teach.title: The word for the person you are talking to

notice.ask: Which word in each sentence is the person being spoken to?

teach.say: When you call somebody by name, or by what they are, that word goes into **the vocative (the calling form)**. It is not the subject and it is not the object — it does no work in the sentence at all. It is the tap on the shoulder, and Latin fences it off with commas, exactly as English does.

check.ask: Which word is the person being spoken to?

teach.title: A word in -us calls with -e
teach.say: Here is the one real change. A second-declension word ending in -us swaps that -us for -e when you call: *Dāvus* becomes *Dāve!*, *servus* becomes *serve!*, *Mārcus* becomes *Mārce!* Nothing else in the word moves.

show.say: serve — -us becomes -e when you call him

teach.title: A name in -ius calls with a single -ī
teach.say: A name ending in -ius does not give *-ie*; it contracts to one long -ī: *Iūlius* → *Iūlī!* The same happens to *fīlius* → *fīlī!* and to *meus* → *mī!*, which is why Ørberg writes *mī fīlī*. Only names and *fīlius* do this. An ordinary word in -ius keeps the -ie: *gladius* becomes *gladie!*

show.say: Iūlī — the -ius of a name contracts to a single -ī

teach.title: Everything else is unchanged
teach.say: Outside those two, the calling form is simply the naming form again. Names in -a do not move (*Syra!*, *Iūlia!*), third-declension words do not move (*pater!*, *māter!*), and no plural ever moves: *puerī* is both 'the boys' and 'boys!'.

show.say: servī — the calling plural, spelt exactly like the naming plural servī

teach.title: Calling him, or talking about him?
teach.say: Two sentences, one name, two jobs. *Mārcus venit* — Marcus is the subject, he is the one coming. *Mārce, venī!* — Marcus is being spoken to and told to come. The -e is not a slip of the pen; it says the word is being addressed, not described.

check.ask: Is *Mēde* the subject of the sentence, or the person being called?

teach.title: What travels with it, and where it sits
teach.say: An adjective beside the person called takes the same ending: *serve improbe!* And the calling form need not come first — Latin often tucks it in after a word or two: *Quid est, domine?*

core.text: When you speak to someone by name or title, that word goes into **the vocative (the calling form)**, *cāsus vocātīvus*: *Salvē, domine!* = Hello, master! *Tacē, Mēde!* Nearly always it looks exactly like the nominative (the plain naming form) — *Iūlia!*, *puerī!* — so there is one thing to learn: nouns in -us change to -e, and names in -ius (and *meus*) to -ī: *Mārce!*, *Iūlī!*, *mī fīlī!*
English marks the person addressed only with commas and the voice: *Bill, the cup is on the table.* Latin gives the name its own ending, which is why *Mārce* looks wrong at first.

Vocative = nominative, except 2nd-declension -us → -e (*serve*, *Dāve*) and a **name** in -ius → -ī (*Iūlī*, and so *fīlī*, *mī*). An ordinary noun in -ius is regular: *gladie*. The plural is never different (*servī!*).

invented.la: Salvē, Iūlī! Ubi est fīlius tuus?
invented.en: Hello, Julius! Where is your son?

invented.la: Ō mī fīlī, venī ad mē!
invented.en: O my son, come to me!

core.text: *Mārcus venit* — Marcus is the subject, coming. *Mārce, venī!* — Marcus is being spoken to and told to come. A name in -e beside a command or a greeting is not a misspelling but the vocative; the subject of the command is 'you'.

more.text: From the learner's notes: direct address is calling out a name to get someone's attention, and it can sit inside a statement, a question or a command. The vocative is left out of most declension charts because it copies the nominative; only the two exceptions need remembering — -us → -e (*Marcus* → *Marce!*), and -ius or *meus* → -ī (*Iūlius* → *Iūlī!*, *meus* → *mī*). The second exception is narrower than it looks: it belongs to *names* in -ius, plus *fīlius* and *genius* (Allen & Greenough §49.c). A common noun in -ius keeps the ordinary -ie — *gladius* → *gladie!*, *fluvius* → *fluvie!*

Ørberg cap. IV: *Dāve!* vocātīvus -e. The vocative often comes second in its sentence, tucked after the first word (*Quid est, domine?*), and can follow *ō* (*Ō Iūlia!*), with the adjectives beside it: *mea parva fīlia*. Adjectives agreeing with it take -e too: *puer improbe!* *Mī* is the vocative of *meus*, but feminine *mea* does not change (*mea Lydia*). *Deus* keeps *deus* as its vocative. A&G §340.
